content: Regimens based on triple therapy (3TC) are considered appropriate for treatment. When using other direct-acting antivirals (DAAs), potential drug-drug interactions must be carefully evaluated. If antiretroviral therapy (ART) is initiated without the inclusion of DAAs, standard first-line ART regimens can be used, provided they do not include zidovudine (AZT), stavudine (d4T), or didanosine (ddI). Efavirenz may also be used, but the dose of telaprevir must be increased accordingly. Boceprevir can be administered alongside raltegravir (RAL), tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), and emtricitabine (FTC). Pharmacokinetic data also support the use of etravirine, rilpivirine, and maraviroc as alternative options. Telaprevir can be combined with either RAL or standard-dose ritonavir-boosted atazanavir (RTV-boosted ATV), with pharmacokinetic data supporting the same alternative agents. Monitoring of CD4 counts is recommended for individuals co-infected with HIV and HCV who are undergoing treatment. HIV-infected individuals are at a higher risk of hematological suppression, which can be a dose-limiting side effect, particularly when certain antiretroviral drugs are co-administered. Additional monitoring may be required for individuals experiencing side effects or those at higher risk, such as those with cirrhosis or those on protease inhibitor (PI) therapy. Liver function monitoring, including albumin, bilirubin, and coagulation tests, is recommended for individuals with cirrhosis. Those with evidence of neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, or anemia require monitoring every 1–2 weeks. In children and adolescents, the prevalence of HCV infection is expected to be higher in regions with a high prevalence of HCV among adults. Treatment is licensed for children older than two years. Pediatric patients treated with pegylated interferon-alpha (PEG-IFNα) and ribavirin (RBV) combination therapy may experience delays in weight and height growth during therapy, but most return to baseline growth percentiles within two years post-treatment. Targeted screening is recommended for children who have undergone medical interventions or received blood products in regions where blood screening is not routine or where sterilization of medical equipment is inadequate. Integrated healthcare is essential for child health, linking maternal and child health services, primary care, and services for people who inject drugs (PWID). Treatment success rates for HCV in children are comparable to those in adults, with sustained virologic response (SVR) rates ranging from 30% to 100%. Adverse effects are primarily flu-like symptoms and neutropenia. For individuals with liver cirrhosis, the disease spectrum ranges from mild fibrosis to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Between 15% and 30% of HCV-infected individuals develop cirrhosis within 20 years, with some progressing to HCC. Treatment with interferon (IFN)-based regimens must begin before decompensated disease onset, as it may precipitate liver failure and death if administered at this stage. Regular clinical examinations and monitoring of serum bilirubin, albumin, and clotting profiles are necessary to detect decompensated disease. Assessment and follow-up for disease progression and HCC are critical for managing HCV-related cirrhosis. Decompensated cirrhosis is associated with life-threatening complications such as ascites, varices, liver failure, renal failure, and sepsis. Co-infection with HBV and HCV can accelerate disease progression, with HCV being the primary driver. Telbivudine, when combined with IFN-containing regimens, may increase the risk of neuropathy. Severe concurrent infections, such as tuberculosis (TB), should generally be treated before initiating HCV therapy. WHO recommends regular TB screening for people living with HIV using a four-symptom algorithm. ART should be initiated as soon as possible in individuals with HIV-associated TB, regardless of CD4 count. Co-management of HCV, HIV, and TB requires careful clinical judgment to minimize additive side effects, pill burden, and drug-drug interactions. In individuals with renal impairment, both RBV and PEG-IFN require dose adjustments. Baseline renal function testing is necessary before initiating therapy. PEG-IFNα2a is cleared by the liver, while PEG-IFNα2b is cleared by the kidneys. Sofosbuvir is excreted by the kidneys, but its safety in individuals with renal impairment is not well-documented. For those with end-stage renal disease, reduced doses of PEG-IFNα2a (135 μg weekly) and RBV are recommended. RBV may be administered at 200 mg daily or every other day in individuals on chronic hemodialysis, as plasma RBV is partially removed during dialysis. Scaling up access to HCV treatment in lowand middle-income countries requires careful consideration of resource availability. High-income models of specialist care with advanced laboratory monitoring are often not feasible in these settings. Service delivery plans must be adapted, drawing on lessons from TB and HIV treatment programs. National programs should estimate the local disease burden and assess available resources and infrastructure for treatment rollout. Sentinel screening of high-risk populations using serology and nucleic acid testing (NAT) is essential for service planning. Improvements in molecular tools for rapid screening, such as dried blood spot and oral fluid testing, would enhance patient identification and expand screening services to hard-to-reach populations. Integration of HCV screening with HIV, HBV, and TB services may be appropriate in many settings due to shared transmission routes. Cost remains a significant barrier to treatment rollout, including the costs of medicines, medical facilities, staff, and diagnostic tools. Negotiation on drug pricing and prioritization of patients with advanced liver disease may be necessary. Task-shifting, where trained personnel such as nurses and pharmacists share clinical responsibilities, can facilitate healthcare delivery. Centralized procurement and the availability of biosimilar or generic formulations can help reduce costs. Clinical and laboratory facilities for screening and monitoring patients on treatment are essential. Simplified methods for assessing HCV viral load and genotype, as well as monitoring drug toxicity, are critical for increasing treatment accessibility in resource-limited settings. Pharmacy facilities and drug storage, including refrigeration for IFN, should be included in treatment center planning. Registration of new drugs in individual countries requires adequate planning. Service delivery should focus on standardized, simplified treatment regimens and decentralized care. Initial clinical assessments are essential to identify conditions that may delay or contraindicate treatment, such as severe intercurrent illnesses, decompensated cirrhosis, or pregnancy. Psychological assessments and evaluation of potential drug-drug interactions are also necessary. Disease education, patient preparation for side effects, and informed counseling are required. Monitoring and evaluation of treatment centers are crucial for appropriate management. Standard registers for tracking progress, similar to those used in TB programs, should be implemented. Increased supervision of sites is likely necessary during the early stages of treatment rollout. The treatment landscape for HCV is rapidly evolving, and adaptations will be required as new drugs are approved. Curative treatments with higher efficacy and lower toxicity have the potential to significantly reduce the global burden of HCV infection. Political will, financial investment, and support from pharmaceutical, medical, and civil society organizations are essential to create widespread access to HCV treatment globally.
